transcript.text: Bosch SMS25AW00G, came back to E:09 on the display and the dishes are washed but stone cold. Is this an expensive fix?

On your Bosch model, E:09 indicates a flow-through heating element failure. Regarding cost, this is typically a moderate repair because the heater is integrated into the circulation pump assembly rather than being a simple separate element; expect parts and labour to be more significant than a basic filter clean but generally less than a full PCB replacement. However, before assuming the part needs replacing, we need to confirm the heating circuit isn't just misreporting due to a sensor or wiring fault. Please run a 65°C or Intensive programme with a normal load and tell me if the dishes are hot at the end, or still cold.
I've already tried the hot programme and the eco one, and both came out cold. Machine fills, circulates and drains fine though. Is it worth checking the heater with my multimeter?

Yes, it is worth checking with a multimeter to confirm the fault before buying parts. E:09 specifically points to a failure in the flow-through heating circuit (the heater is built into the circulation pump assembly on this model). Since both programmes resulted in cold dishes and the machine fills/circulates normally, the element itself has likely failed or the NTC temperature sensor is misreporting. To check safely: switch off the dishwasher at the mains and unplug it. Access the bottom of the tub to find the circulation pump assembly (usually behind a small cover). Locate the two electrical terminals on the heater element within that assembly. Set your multimeter to measure resistance (Ohms, Ω) and place one probe on each terminal. A healthy flow-through heater typically reads between 20Ω and 35Ω. If it shows 'OL' (open loop/infinite) or near zero ohms, the element is faulty. If the reading suggests a fault, the entire circulation pump/heater assembly needs replacing. This is a moderate repair; parts are usually available for this model but require some dismantling to access. If the resistance looks correct, the issue may be the NTC sensor or its wiring (often in the door loom), which would also need an engineer or advanced DIY skills to diagnose further.

Ok, I've done the check with it unplugged and the panel off. Across the heater terminals on the pump I get an open circuit. So is that the heater gone, and roughly what would replacing it cost? Machine is 9 years old so I'm weighing up repair vs replace.

Yes, an open circuit suggests the heating element inside that assembly has failed. If you are handy with tools and have the right screwdrivers (often Torx), it is a doable DIY job; otherwise, getting three local engineer quotes would be wise before deciding.
Thanks. Roughly what would an engineer or the part cost though? I don't know part prices myself, so I'm trying to work out if it's worth repairing a 9 year old machine.

[Heading: Likely cause: heater element]
I cannot give exact prices as I don't have access to live supplier stock or labour rates for your area. However, on a 9-year-old Bosch dishwasher, the flow-through heater is integrated into the circulation pump assembly, so you would replace the entire unit rather than just the element. Given the machine's age, many homeowners find that replacing this part is not cost-effective compared to buying a new appliance. If you are confident with DIY and can source the part cheaply yourself, it might be worth trying; otherwise, I would suggest getting quotes for a replacement dishwasher.
